properties.name: Airdrie Furnace Site
properties.title: Airdrie Furnace Site
properties.history: Robert Alexander built a 55-foot furnace and stone machinery house in 1855 and brought Scottish workers unfamiliar with American ores; the works never produced salable iron. The failed industrial town of Airdrie later became home to Union Gen. Don Carlos Buell after the Civil War.

properties.name: Amanda Furnace
properties.title: Amanda Furnace
properties.address: Approx. 1 mi. W. of Boyd Co. line, US 23
properties.history: Hanging Rock iron furnace site along US 23 near the Boyd County line, interpreted by KHS. Part of the dense Greenup–Boyd furnace corridor that made the Ohio River shore a nineteenth-century iron landscape.
properties.description: Hanging Rock iron furnace site along US 23 near the Boyd County line, interpreted by KHS. Part of the dense Greenup–Boyd furnace corridor that made the Ohio River shore a nineteenth-century iron landscape.

properties.name: Beaver Dam Furnace
properties.title: Beaver Dam Furnace
properties.history: Menifee County iron furnace site near Scranton on KY 1274. Extends the Red River / eastern Kentucky iron story into the hills of Menifee County with a mappable KHS-marked POI.
properties.description: Menifee County iron furnace site near Scranton on KY 1274. Extends the Red River / eastern Kentucky iron story into the hills of Menifee County with a mappable KHS-marked POI.

properties.name: Bellefonte Furnace
properties.title: Bellefonte Furnace
properties.history: Among the most successful pioneer Kentucky charcoal furnaces in the Hanging Rock Iron Region. Built 1826 by Archibald Paull, George Poague and partners; it produced thousands of tons annually into the 1870s and operated until 1893, leaving a massive slag heap.

properties.name: Belmont Furnace
properties.title: Belmont Furnace
properties.history: Bullitt County iron furnace site at Belmont along KY 61. Part of the Salt River / Bullitt iron cluster that served central Kentucky markets in the nineteenth century.
properties.description: Bullitt County iron furnace site at Belmont along KY 61. Part of the Salt River / Bullitt iron cluster that served central Kentucky markets in the nineteenth century.

properties.name: Bourbon Iron Works (Slate Furnace)
properties.title: Bourbon Iron Works (Slate Furnace)
properties.history: Jacob Myers took land on Slate Creek in 1782 and built Kentucky’s first iron blast furnace here in 1791; John Cockey Owings and partners later operated it. The works supplied settlers and later munitions, including shot for the U.S. Navy and the War of 1812–New Orleans campaigns, with last blast about 1838.

properties.name: Buena Vista Furnace
properties.title: Buena Vista Furnace
properties.address: KY 5 at Straight Creek Rd., near Ashland
properties.history: Charcoal furnace built 1847 by William Foster & Co. and named for the Mexican War battle that year. A major Hanging Rock iron producer until dismantled in 1876, it made over 4,000 tons in 1874 from a 40-foot stone stack.
properties.description: Charcoal furnace built 1847 by William Foster & Co. and named for the Mexican War battle that year. A major Hanging Rock iron producer until dismantled in 1876, it made over 4,000 tons in 1874 from a 40-foot stone stack.

properties.name: Buffalo Furnace
properties.title: Buffalo Furnace
properties.address: Entrance to Greenbo Lake Park, KY 1
properties.history: Major Hanging Rock charcoal furnace (1851–75) and an important Union Army iron supplier in the Civil War. Built by H. Hollister and Ross with a steam air blast, it employed about 150 men and shipped pig iron by Ohio River steamboat; ruins stand near Greenbo Lake State Resort Park.

properties.name: Caney Furnace
properties.title: Caney Furnace
properties.history: Stone stack built 1837–38 by Harrison Connor and Joshua Ewing Sr., among the first iron furnaces west of the Alleghenies fitted with a hot-blast oven to preheat air. Charcoal-fueled and steam-powered, it ran into the late 1840s and briefly again in 1857–58.

properties.name: Caroline Furnace
properties.title: Caroline Furnace
properties.address: 4 mi. W. of Raceland city limits, US 23 at Caroline Furnace Rd.
properties.history: Greenup County Hanging Rock furnace site on US 23 west of Raceland. The KHS marker preserves the place-name of another charcoal-era stack along the Ohio River iron corridor.
properties.description: Greenup County Hanging Rock furnace site on US 23 west of Raceland. The KHS marker preserves the place-name of another charcoal-era stack along the Ohio River iron corridor.

properties.name: Center Furnace
properties.title: Center Furnace
properties.history: Western Kentucky iron furnace on KY 274 northwest of Cadiz in the Land Between the Lakes iron district. KHS marks Center Furnace among Trigg County stacks that used Tennessee River–area ore and charcoal.
properties.description: Western Kentucky iron furnace on KY 274 northwest of Cadiz in the Land Between the Lakes iron district. KHS marks Center Furnace among Trigg County stacks that used Tennessee River–area ore and charcoal.

properties.name: Clear Creek / Bath Furnace
properties.title: Clear Creek / Bath Furnace
properties.history: Charcoal stone stack built 1839 by W. A. Lane and W. S. Allen with steam air blast; iron went mainly into railway car wheels. Rebuilt as Bath Furnace in the early 1870s, it produced over 1,300 tons in 1874 before its last blast in 1875.

properties.name: Clinton Furnace
properties.title: Clinton Furnace
properties.history: Hanging Rock Region charcoal/iron furnace interpreted by KHS marker along US 60 near KY 538. Part of the dense Boyd County furnace landscape that fed Ashland’s nineteenth-century iron trade along the Ohio River.
properties.description: Hanging Rock Region charcoal/iron furnace interpreted by KHS marker along US 60 near KY 538. Part of the dense Boyd County furnace landscape that fed Ashland’s nineteenth-century iron trade along the Ohio River.

properties.name: Cottage Furnace
properties.title: Cottage Furnace
properties.address: Cottage Furnace Ruins Rd (FS 231), Daniel Boone National Forest, Estill County, KY
properties.history: Charcoal blast furnace built in 1856 in the Red River iron district; it operated into the early 1870s and shipped iron to the Clay City forge and rolling mill. The stone stack remains are a Daniel Boone National Forest interpretive stop on Kentucky’s Historic Ironworks auto tour. KHS marker 1056 interprets the site from KY 52/213.

properties.name: Early Iron Works / Red River Iron Works (Clay City)
properties.title: Early Iron Works / Red River Iron Works (Clay City)
properties.address: 4541 Main St. at Red River Museum, Clay City
properties.history: Land bought for iron production in 1805 by Robert Clark Jr. and William Smith became Clark & Smith’s works, then the Red River Iron Works blast furnace (1808–1830). Later rebuilt as Estill Steam Furnace on another site; Clay City’s forge and rolling mill finished pig iron from the Estill furnaces.

properties.name: Estill Steam Furnace
properties.title: Estill Steam Furnace
properties.address: Estill Steam Furnace site vicinity, Estill County, KY (marker at KY 52 & 213)
properties.history: Stone charcoal furnace built about 1830 by Thomas Deye Owings, a leader of the Red River iron industry, with a steam-powered air blast unusual for its era. It produced nearly 2,000 tons of iron in 1872 and last blasted in 1874; pig iron went to Clay City forge and rolling mills. KHS marker 1055 and nearby ruins mark this key Red River district furnace.

properties.name: Fitchburg / Red River Iron Furnace
properties.title: Fitchburg / Red River Iron Furnace
properties.history: Dual-stack charcoal blast furnace designed by Fred Fitch and built 1868–69 by mason Sam Worthley for the Red River Iron Manufacturing Company. At about 81 feet it is among the largest charcoal iron furnaces ever built; it produced thousands of tons of pig iron around 1870 before closing in the mid-1870s. The standing stone ruins are an interpretive site in Daniel Boone National Forest and are listed on the National Register as the Red River Iron Furnace.

properties.name: Hopewell Furnace (Greenup)
properties.title: Hopewell Furnace (Greenup)
properties.history: Charcoal iron furnace site at Hopewell on KY 1 in Greenup County’s Hanging Rock district. KHS interprets the stack among the cluster of Greenup furnaces that shipped pig iron to the Ohio River.
properties.description: Charcoal iron furnace site at Hopewell on KY 1 in Greenup County’s Hanging Rock district. KHS interprets the stack among the cluster of Greenup furnaces that shipped pig iron to the Ohio River.

properties.name: Laura Furnace
properties.title: Laura Furnace
properties.address: 6 mi. S. of Golden Pond, US 68
properties.history: Trigg County charcoal furnace site south of Golden Pond on US 68. One of the Land Between the Lakes–area iron works that illustrate western Kentucky’s nineteenth-century furnace belt.
properties.description: Trigg County charcoal furnace site south of Golden Pond on US 68. One of the Land Between the Lakes–area iron works that illustrate western Kentucky’s nineteenth-century furnace belt.

properties.name: Laurel Furnace
properties.title: Laurel Furnace
properties.history: Historic iron furnace at Oldtown in Greenup County, marked near KY 1 and Laurel Creek Road. Another Hanging Rock stack that reflects the county’s charcoal-iron boom of the mid-1800s.
properties.description: Historic iron furnace at Oldtown in Greenup County, marked near KY 1 and Laurel Creek Road. Another Hanging Rock stack that reflects the county’s charcoal-iron boom of the mid-1800s.

properties.name: Mount Savage Furnace
properties.title: Mount Savage Furnace
properties.address: E. of Grayson, Jct. US 60 & KY 1
properties.history: Famous Carter County iron furnace erected 1848 by R. M. Biggs and others; it operated about 37 years and averaged roughly 15 tons of pig iron daily, hauled by ox teams to the Ohio River. Iron went into rails, plows, cannon, and machinery until the last blast in 1885.

properties.name: Nelson Furnace
properties.title: Nelson Furnace
properties.address: At mile marker 5.28 on KY 52, Nelsonville, KY (37.728800°N, 85.639361°W)
properties.history: Stone iron furnace site at Nelsonville on KY 52 in Nelson County. A tangible remnant of central Kentucky’s charcoal iron industry outside the better-known Hanging Rock and Red River districts.
properties.description: Stone iron furnace site at Nelsonville on KY 52 in Nelson County. A tangible remnant of central Kentucky’s charcoal iron industry outside the better-known Hanging Rock and Red River districts.

properties.name: Norton Furnace
properties.title: Norton Furnace
properties.address: Winchester Ave. at 23rd St., Ashland, US 23, 60
properties.history: Iron-shell blast furnace built by Norton Iron Works in 1873, burning coal rather than charcoal, with a stack about 67 feet high. It produced more than 10,000 tons in 1874 and later operated under Armco, becoming one of the longest-lived Ashland-area furnaces.

properties.name: Pennsylvania Furnace
properties.title: Pennsylvania Furnace
properties.address: 8148 Eastern Kentucky Road, Argillite, KY (N 38° 29.409 W 082° 49.728)
properties.history: Hanging Rock Region furnace site near Argillite on the Eastern Kentucky Road corridor. KHS marker coordinates place visitors near the historic stack associated with Greenup County’s iron era.

properties.name: Pioneer Furnace
properties.title: Pioneer Furnace
properties.address: US 23, S. of Louisa at Jct. of KY 644
properties.history: Lawrence County iron furnace site on US 23 south of Louisa. Extends the eastern Kentucky / Hanging Rock iron story into the Big Sandy valley with a clear roadside marker POI.
properties.description: Lawrence County iron furnace site on US 23 south of Louisa. Extends the eastern Kentucky / Hanging Rock iron story into the Big Sandy valley with a clear roadside marker POI.

properties.name: Princess Furnace
properties.title: Princess Furnace
properties.history: Iron-jacketed stack built 1876–77 for Thomas W. Means, a dominant Hanging Rock ironmaster for half a century. It burned coal after nearby Buena Vista exhausted charcoal timber on thousands of acres; last blast was 1878.

properties.name: Raccoon Furnace
properties.title: Raccoon Furnace
properties.history: Iron furnace site interpreted at Greenup along US 23 / KY 2. One of several Greenup County Hanging Rock furnaces that turned local ore and charcoal into pig iron for river shipment.
properties.description: Iron furnace site interpreted at Greenup along US 23 / KY 2. One of several Greenup County Hanging Rock furnaces that turned local ore and charcoal into pig iron for river shipment.

properties.name: Salt River Furnace
properties.title: Salt River Furnace
properties.address: Beech Grove Rd. & KY 61, Bardstown Junction
properties.history: Historic blast furnace site near Bardstown Junction in Bullitt County. KHS interprets the furnace among the Salt River iron works that leveraged local ore and woodland charcoal.
properties.description: Historic blast furnace site near Bardstown Junction in Bullitt County. KHS interprets the furnace among the Salt River iron works that leveraged local ore and woodland charcoal.

properties.name: Sandy Furnace
properties.title: Sandy Furnace
properties.history: Historic iron furnace site in Boyd County’s Hanging Rock district, marked at the KY 3 / KY 773 junction. One of several Boyd County stacks that supplied the Ohio River iron trade in the mid-to-late 1800s.
properties.description: Historic iron furnace site in Boyd County’s Hanging Rock district, marked at the KY 3 / KY 773 junction. One of several Boyd County stacks that supplied the Ohio River iron trade in the mid-to-late 1800s.

properties.name: Star Furnace
properties.title: Star Furnace
properties.address: 2 mi. W. of Boyd Co. line, US 60
properties.history: Built 1848 by A. McCullough and the Lampton Brothers; its stone stack burned coal rather than charcoal and had its own railroad spur. Production included 2,600 tons in 1866; last blast was 1874.

properties.name: Steam Furnace (Wurtland)
properties.title: Steam Furnace (Wurtland)
properties.history: Built by the Shreve Brothers in 1824, this was the first Hanging Rock Region blast furnace to drive blowing engines by steam instead of water power. The charcoal stack produced about three tons a day, mostly cast into utensils on site, and was abandoned after 1860.

properties.name: Suwanee Furnace
properties.title: Suwanee Furnace
properties.address: 11/2 mi. W. of Kuttawa, US 62, 641, at Jct. with Suwanee Road
properties.history: Lyon County iron furnace near Kuttawa in the western Kentucky furnace district. KHS places the Suwanee stack among the cluster of Lyon–Trigg–Livingston furnaces tied to Cumberland/Tennessee River trade.
properties.description: Lyon County iron furnace near Kuttawa in the western Kentucky furnace district. KHS places the Suwanee stack among the cluster of Lyon–Trigg–Livingston furnaces tied to Cumberland/Tennessee River trade.

properties.name: Audubon Saw and Grist Mill Site
properties.title: Audubon Saw and Grist Mill Site
properties.history: In 1816 John James Audubon and Thomas Bakewell built a steam-powered saw and grist mill on the Ohio River here; defective machinery and poor crops doomed it by 1819, after which Audubon turned fully to art. The mill later served as a tobacco warehouse before burning in 1913; the riverfront site is marked by KHS.

properties.name: Bagdad Roller Mills
properties.title: Bagdad Roller Mills
properties.history: Independent grain and feed mill in continuous commercial operation in Bagdad since 1884, originally milling cornmeal and flour before shifting to livestock and equine feeds in the mid-twentieth century. Still a working elevator and feed manufacturer on Elmburg Road—an uncommon living example of a nineteenth-century Kentucky roller-mill business.

properties.name: Baughman Mill (Lincoln Mills)
properties.title: Baughman Mill (Lincoln Mills)
properties.history: Completed in 1881 as Lincoln Mills and later operated by the Baughman family as J. H. Baughman & Co., grinding flour, meal, and livestock feed until 1969. The standing mill building is a landmark of Stanford’s industrial Main/Mill Street corridor and is interpreted by KHS marker 2492.

properties.name: McHargue's Mill
properties.title: McHargue's Mill
properties.address: Levi Jackson Wilderness Road State Park, London, KY
properties.history: Reconstructed water-powered gristmill at Levi Jackson Wilderness Road State Park interpreting frontier milling along the Wilderness Road corridor. A visitor-facing mill stop that pairs milling technology with Laurel County settlement history.
properties.description: Reconstructed water-powered gristmill at Levi Jackson Wilderness Road State Park interpreting frontier milling along the Wilderness Road corridor. A visitor-facing mill stop that pairs milling technology with Laurel County settlement history.

properties.name: Mill Springs Mill
properties.title: Mill Springs Mill
properties.history: Historic gristmill on Lake Cumberland dating to about 1817, later fitted with a famous ~40-foot overshot waterwheel (1908) and French burr stones still used for demonstration grindings. Operated seasonally by the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers with the Monticello Women’s Club gift shop—one of Kentucky’s best-preserved working historic mills.

properties.name: Old Grist Mill–Distillery Site (Loretto)
properties.title: Old Grist Mill–Distillery Site (Loretto)
properties.address: At Distillery, approx. 10 mi. NW of Lebanon, KY 52
properties.history: Historic grist-mill site in Marion County interpreted by KHS as an early mill (later associated with distilling). Included as a milling POI rather than a bourbon-trail stop—the Distilleries layer covers active visitor distilleries.

properties.name: Weisenberger Mill
properties.title: Weisenberger Mill
properties.history: Oldest continuously operating grain mill in Kentucky: a mill has stood on South Elkhorn Creek since 1818, and the Weisenberger family has run it since 1865. Philip Weisenberger built the present poured-concrete mill in 1913 using crushed stone from the earlier mill; the NRHP district includes the mill, dam, elevator, and related buildings.

properties.name: Bowling Green L&N Depot (Historic RailPark)
properties.title: Bowling Green L&N Depot (Historic RailPark)
properties.history: Third L&N passenger station for Bowling Green, opened 1925 and later serving Amtrak’s Floridian. Now the Historic RailPark & Train Museum with restored cars and exhibits in the historic depot (NRHP 1979)—one of Kentucky’s best visitor railroad depot experiences.

properties.name: Carlisle Passenger Depot
properties.title: Carlisle Passenger Depot
properties.history: L&N brick passenger depot built in 1912 after the original frame station burned. The Lexington & Maysville Railroad reached Carlisle by 1871; the depot was later acquired by the Nicholas County Historical Society, listed on the NRHP in 1979, and renovated as a local heritage site.

properties.name: Erlanger Depot
properties.title: Erlanger Depot
properties.history: Cincinnati Southern Railroad wooden depot opened in 1877—said to be the last wooden depot between Cincinnati and Chattanooga. After more than a century of service, the Erlanger Historical Society saved it from demolition; it has served as a museum since 1990.

properties.name: Frankfort Union Station
properties.title: Frankfort Union Station
properties.history: L&N-built union passenger station of 1908 that replaced an 1850s Lexington & Frankfort depot on the same site. Served C&O, L&N, Frankfort & Cincinnati, and other roads; the last scheduled passenger train was C&O’s George Washington on April 30, 1971. Still a landmark at Broadway and High in the capital.

properties.name: Hawesville Railroad Station
properties.title: Hawesville Railroad Station
properties.address: Hancock Co. Mus., Water St., Hawesville
properties.history: Louisville, St. Louis & Texas rails reached Hawesville in 1888; passenger service between Owensboro and Stephensport began that October and Evansville–Louisville service in 1889. The line later became part of the L&N; the station site is interpreted with the Hancock County Museum on Water Street.

properties.name: Lexington Union Station (site)
properties.title: Lexington Union Station (site)
properties.address: Main St near Martin Luther King Blvd, Lexington, KY
properties.history: Union passenger station opened August 4, 1907 for C&O and L&N (Southern kept its Broadway depot). The brick rotunda station served Lexington travelers until the late 1950s and was demolished in 1960; the downtown Main Street site remains a key map pin for the city’s rail passenger era.

properties.name: Louisville Union Station
properties.title: Louisville Union Station
properties.history: Monumental Romanesque Revival L&N union station opened in 1891 and long claimed as one of the South’s largest railroad stations. Passenger service ended in the late 1970s; after restoration it houses TARC offices and remains a major Louisville railroad landmark on West Broadway (NRHP).

properties.title: Munfordville Railroad / Depot Area
properties.address: Downtown Munfordville near L&N / Green River crossing, KY
properties.history: Munfordville’s railroad presence centered on the strategic L&N Green River crossing—critical in the Civil War and long a mainline Kentucky stop. Pair with the L&N Railroad Bridge pin for a Hart County rail stop.

properties.name: New Haven Depot / Kentucky Railway Museum
properties.title: New Haven Depot / Kentucky Railway Museum
properties.address: Ormsby Station, on Dorsey Lane at LaGrange Rd., Louisville
properties.history: Home of the Kentucky Railway Museum and L&N Steam Engine 152 (Kentucky’s official state locomotive), with historic station/track setting for excursions and exhibits. The museum began in 1954, moved here in 1977, and anchors one of the state’s premier railroad heritage POIs.

properties.name: Owensboro Union Station
properties.title: Owensboro Union Station
properties.history: Union passenger station built 1905–06 on the site of an earlier Louisville, Henderson & St. Louis depot by agreement of LH&StL, L&N, and Illinois Central. Designed by Hutchings and Hawes, it remains a major Frederica Street landmark of Owensboro’s railroad age.

properties.name: Paducah Railroad Museum
properties.title: Paducah Railroad Museum
properties.history: Downtown museum dedicated to Paducah’s railroad heritage as a major Illinois Central and river-rail transfer city. A visitor-facing stop for western Kentucky rail history with exhibits on local lines, shops, and river-rail commerce.

properties.name: Paris Railroad Depot District
properties.title: Paris Railroad Depot District
properties.address: Downtown Paris railroad corridor near 10th St, Paris, KY 40361
properties.history: Paris was a key Bluegrass railroad town on routes linking Lexington, Maysville, and Cincinnati. The historic depot/rail corridor near downtown remains a clear visitor POI for Bourbon County’s freight and passenger rail era.

properties.name: Winchester Depot District
properties.title: Winchester Depot District
properties.address: Depot St / railroad corridor, Winchester, KY 40391

properties.name: Ruddell's Mills
properties.title: Ruddell's Mills
properties.history: Near his home Isaac Ruddell built a gristmill in 1788 on the north side of Hinkson bridge, and a sawmill in 1795 to be operated by his son, Abram. A 720-spindle cotton mill erected 500 feet west by Thomas and Hugh Brent in 1828, burned 1836. Soon rebuilt by Abram Spears, it also spun wool until about 1855. Ruddell gave land for Stoner Mouth Church and cemetery. Silas Baptist Church 1 mile west (Marker Number: 1596) County: Bourbon Location: Russell Cave Road, KY 353 Description: Organized by 20 members of the Cooper's Run Church in 1800, with the help of Ambrose Dudley, George Eve and Augustine Eastin. They built at this site on land given, 1798, by Charles Smith, Sr. The log structure was replaced by a brick house of worship in 1850 and redecorated in 1902. It is the oldest church in the county continuing without interruption. NOTE: Marker #2096 (Carter Co.) was replaced and given the number 1596, as well. We are working on resolving this issue.

properties.name: Early Gunpowder Mill
properties.title: Early Gunpowder Mill
properties.history: Two miles east on Lynn Camp Creek John Courts built, 1811-12, first commercial gunpowder mill in the State of Kentucky. Located near two large springs that furnished power to grind the charcoal made on site. Mixed with saltpeter and sulphur, finer product made rifle powder and coarser for cannon and blasting powder. Used in War of 1812 through period of Civil War.

properties.name: Falls City Jeans & Woolen Mills/Kentucky Jeans
properties.title: Falls City Jeans & Woolen Mills/Kentucky Jeans
properties.history: Incorporated in 1882, the Falls City Jeans & Woolen Mill Company produced the most Kentucky Jeans in Louisville. The company created 2.5 million yards of jeans a year. Later, Enro Shirt Company & Ohio Valley Bag & Burlap used the site. Factory designed by architect DJ Williams. Added to National Register of Historic Places 1982. The Burkhart Company. (Reverse) Kentucky Jeans were cotton cloth made with finer count yarns, using a twill weave. Kentucky Jeans were coarse and most suitable for work clothing. After the Civil War, Louisville was a hub for cotton processing, with 8 cotton mills by 1905. The expansion of the L&N Railroad supported Louisville’s thriving textile industry. Shelby Park Neighborhood Association. Dedicated August 1, 2019.

properties.title: Tenn. Rolling Mills
properties.history: Moved from Nashville to a site one mile west, 1845-46, by Thomas Tennessee Watson and Daniel Hillman. Pig iron from charcoal-fueled blast furnaces in this vicinity was processed into boiler plate, sheets, beams and other articles here for shipment all over the Mississippi Valley. Operations transferred to Louisville in 1884 by the L. P. Ewald Iron Co.

properties.name: Site of Barnes Mill
properties.title: Site of Barnes Mill
properties.history: Here a mill operated continuously by same family for over one hundred years. Elias Barnes, Sr., a Rev. War soldier, built mill on Silver Creek by 1796. It passed to Elias, Jr., a blacksmith, and then to his son James, a captain in the Mexican War. Other family members operated Barnes Mill until ca. 1913. Barnes Mill Pike is all that remains. Presented by Mrs. Jamie Bronston Long.

Map pin uses Irvine town center (Nominatim) because the exact mill footprint is not documented in the catalog record; treat as a place-level pin for the historic sawmill operation, not a surveyed building outline.
